home_feat_failure_desc: Narrow down why a part broke from its fracture surface and service
about_failure: answer questions about fracture features and service conditions to see candidate failure modes, how to tell them apart and how to prevent them, plus case studies of accidents caused by material failures.
failure_look: How to recognize it (fracture surface, microstructure, SEM)
failure_score_for: Clues that score for this mode
failure_table_combo: Combination points (added when both are selected)
failure_empty: Answer the questions and the candidate failure modes will be listed here, with the clues behind each one.

failure_next: Answering “{q}” next will help separate {a} from {b}.
failure_unlikely: Modes that do not fit your current answers
failure_none_fit: No failure mode has a positive score with these answers. Review your answers or set some back to “Don’t know”.

failure_url_note: Your answers are kept in this page’s URL, so the link opens the same answers and candidates. Nothing is sent to a server.

home_feat_atlas_desc: Compare metal microstructures as schematics; learn to identify them and measure grain size
about_atlas: compare metal microstructures such as ferrite, pearlite, martensite and graphite in cast iron as schematic drawings, with their features, how they form, how they look after etching and how to tell them apart, plus a grain size number converter and an identification quiz.
atlas_noscript: The schematics, grain size converter and quiz need JavaScript. The text can be read without it.
atlas_list_lead: {n} microstructures, grouped by how they form. Tap a drawing to open how to identify it.
atlas_entries_lead: Tap a name to open its schematic, what you see, how it forms and how to tell it from look-alikes.
atlas_frac_hypo: Steel with {c}% C: mass fraction of pearlite by the lever rule {p}%
atlas_frac_hyper: Steel with {c}% C: mass fraction of proeutectoid cementite by the lever rule {p}%
atlas_shade: Why it looks light or dark
atlas_forms: How it forms (alloy and heat treatment)
atlas_confuse: Look-alikes and how to tell them apart
atlas_link_grain: Copy link to this grain size
atlas_grain_h: Grain size (grain size number and mean grain size)
atlas_grain_cmp: The idea of the comparison method
atlas_grain_cmp_lead: Grains one number apart, drawn at the same magnification. In the comparison method you match the specimen against standard charts like these.
atlas_g_cap: Schematic. Approx. magnification ×{m} (field width {w}), the equivalent of {n} grains in the field area
atlas_g_d: Mean grain diameter (square root of mean area)
atlas_g_n100: Grains per square inch at 100× (ASTM N)
atlas_g_count: Count the grains in the drawing
atlas_g_jeff: Planimetric: {i} grains inside + {c} grains cut by the frame × 1/2 + 1 for the corners = {n}. Divided by the field area {a} mm² gives {na} grains/mm² → G = {g}
atlas_g_icpt: Intercept: total test line length (dashed) {L} mm with {p} grain boundary intersections → ℓ̄ = {l} mm → G = {g}
atlas_g_count_note: The drawing uses {na} grains per mm² (the equivalent of {n} grains in the field area), and the grains continue beyond the frame. The counts give slightly different numbers because only a limited number of grains is counted and because of the grain shapes (see the note below).
atlas_practice_lead: Look at the schematic and choose the microstructure. After you answer you get the identification clues and how to tell it from the one you chose. The drawing changes a little every time.
atlas_p_shared: This question came from a shared link. This answer is not added to your record.
atlas_p_nostore: This browser cannot save the record; it will be lost when you close the page.
atlas_url_note: Your record stays in this browser and is never sent anywhere. A link copied before answering lets the recipient solve the same drawing; a link copied after answering opens your choice and the result.
home_feat_drill_desc: Practice calculation problems with new numbers every time, with worked steps
about_drill: practice standard materials science calculations, such as interplanar spacing, the lever rule, diffusion, fracture toughness and thermal stress, with new numbers each time. Answers are marked with units, with worked steps and the common mistake your number points to.
drill_noscript: Generating and marking problems needs JavaScript. You can still read the list of problem types and the notes on solving, units and significant figures below.
drill_answer_in: Give about {sig} significant figures. Tolerance ±{tol} %. Forms such as 2.3e-5 and 2.3×10^-5 are accepted.
drill_bad_input: That is not a number I can read. Examples: 0.287, 2.3e-5, 2.3×10^-5
drill_bad_unit: Unknown unit “{u}”. Choose the unit from the menu.
drill_h_sign: The sign is reversed. Check tension versus compression, or increase versus decrease.
drill_h_unit: This looks like a unit mix-up: your number is the value in {u}. In {uu} it is {a}.
drill_h_pow: You are off by a factor of 10^{n}. Check unit conversions (mm and m, kJ and J, cm³ and m³ and so on).
drill_h_close: Close, but outside the ±{tol} % tolerance. You may have rounded intermediate values too much or used a different constant from the problem.
drill_h_either: This value matches more than one common mistake (any of these is possible):
drill_tool_lead: Check it in the calculator, filled in with the same numbers:
drill_url_note: The URL holds only the problem type and a seed (?t=…&s=…), never the answer. Your record is saved only in this browser.
drill_sum_again: Another set with the same settings
drill_rec_empty: No record yet. Results are saved only in this browser.
drill_rec_clear_q: Clear the calculation drill record saved in this browser?
drill_types_lead: Click a type to get one problem of that type. Click a field name to start with that field selected.
home_feat_materials_desc: Find, compare and export property values with sources
about_materials: look up density, Young’s modulus, strength, thermal conductivity, thermal expansion, melting point, lattice constants and more for metals, ceramics, polymers, composite fibers and semiconductors, each value with its source and conditions. Switch units, compare 2–4 materials side by side and export CSV with a source column.
md_noscript: Search, filters, unit switching, comparison and CSV need JavaScript. The table below lists the main properties in the default units.
md_static_note: With JavaScript you can search, filter, sort and switch units in this table.
md_share_note: The URL keeps the search, filters, columns, units, sort, compared materials and the open card.
md_empty: No material matches. Shorten the search or reset the filters.
md_table_lead: Superscript numbers are source numbers (see the source list below); small text gives the grade, state, kind of strength and condition. “+n” is the number of other values for the same property: click the material name to see all of them on its card. Ranges show “low–high” and the representative value. Click a column heading to sort.
md_open_tool_note: Opens the calculator with this material’s values filled in.
md_cmp_lead: Materials ticked in the left column of the table (2–4) are lined up property by property.
md_cmp_empty: No material selected yet. Tick the left column of the table or use “Add to comparison” on a card.
md_cmp_one: {m} selected. Select at least one more to compare.
md_cmp_lead2: Ratios (×) take the first material ({m}) as 1. Ranges are compared by their representative values. Each material is compared by the first value shown in the table.
md_cmp_kind: Different kinds of strength ({l}). Compare ratios only between the same kind.
md_cmp_range: A range’s representative value is compared with a single value.
md_cmp_kelvin: Temperature ratios are calculated in kelvin.
md_cmp_nobase: The first material has no value here, so no ratio is shown.
md_cmp_max: You can compare up to 4 materials.
md_csv_wide: As in the table (one material per row; value, range, condition and source per column)
md_csv_long: All values (one value per row, with the value in its original unit)
md_csv_note: Exports the filtered materials in the displayed units (numbers keep the significant figures of the original values). The source column gives the name of each source.
md_chart_lead: The filtered materials, in descending order of the chosen property (up to 40). Lines are ranges; dots are representative or single values. Click a bar to open the material’s card.
md_chart_none: None of the filtered materials has a value for this property.
md_sources_lead: Numbers match the source numbers in the table and on the cards. Parentheses name the calculator that uses the values.
home_feat_formulas_desc: {n} materials science formulas with symbols, units, conditions and examples. Print only the ones you pick
about_formulas: materials science formulas with symbols and SI units, conditions of use, common mistakes and a numerical example, with the dimensions of every formula checked by machine. Print the formulas you pick as an A4 sheet, or share them as a link.
formulas_noscript: Search, filtering, picking and printing need JavaScript. All formulas are listed on this page.
formulas_search_ph: Name, symbol or term (e.g. Bragg, K_IC, diffusion length)
formulas_none: No formula matches. Try a shorter word or set the topic to “All”.
formulas_pick_first: Tick “Pick” on the formulas you want to print first.
formulas_sel_note: Your picks are kept in this browser only and never sent to a server.
formulas_dim_ok: both sides agree on every line ([ ] in SI base units)
home_feat_methods_desc: Narrow down {n} analysis and testing methods by what you want to know and what your sample allows, then compare them
about_methods: analysis and testing methods such as SEM, XRD, XPS, SIMS, hardness testing and ultrasonic testing, narrowed down by what you want to know and what the sample allows (destructive or not, size, conductivity, elements, resolution, depth). Methods that do not fit are set aside with the reason, and 2–4 methods can be compared side by side. The conditions can be shared as a link.
methods_noscript: Filtering and the side-by-side table need JavaScript. All method descriptions and the overview table are on this page.
methods_need_label: What do you want to know?
methods_d_cut: Cutting and polishing are fine (no dissolving or breaking)
methods_m_metal: Non-magnetic metal (Al, Cu, austenitic stainless steel, etc.)
methods_v: Cannot go into vacuum (contains water or oil, or outgasses)
methods_z_n: Down to tens of µm (thin films, platings, oxide layers)
methods_count: {n} of the {m} methods for this purpose fit the conditions (best first)
methods_count_all: {n} of all {m} methods fit the conditions
methods_none: No method fits. Try removing conditions one at a time; the reasons are listed under “Methods that do not fit”.
methods_why_ds1: The sample has to be cut or polished
methods_why_ds2: The sample is dissolved or broken
methods_why_small: The sample is too small for this method
methods_why_big: A large part does not fit as it is (it has to be cut)
methods_why_cond: Works only on electrically conductive materials
methods_why_vac: The sample has to go into vacuum
methods_why_nocno: Cannot measure light elements (C, N, O)
methods_why_dl: The detection limit is too high for trace levels
methods_why_avg: Gives an average over the sample, not values at each spot
methods_why_resna: Not a method rated by spatial resolution
methods_why_res: Lateral resolution is not fine enough
methods_why_depth: Does not probe the depth of interest
methods_nb_cutout: Large parts have to be cut to fit
methods_nb_lowvac: The sample goes into vacuum or reduced pressure (check that it can tolerate this)
methods_nb_dl4: The detection limit is only about 100 ppm (less is hard to see)
methods_cmp_empty: Tick “Compare” on 2–4 methods to see them side by side here.
methods_cmp_one: Pick at least one more method to compare.
methods_cmp_max: You can compare up to 4 methods.
methods_table_lead: Resolution, detection limit, and whether the sample is destroyed, preparation, time and cost for every method in one table. Figures are typical ranges and vary with the instrument and conditions. Preparation, time and cost are rough three-level comparisons between methods; actual prices and turnaround depend on the laboratory.
methods_z_m: Layer 0.1 to a few mm deep (carburizing, decarburization, peening)
methods_why_ds1by: For this purpose or depth the sample has to be sputtered or cut (sections, depth profiles, layer removal)
methods_why_nometal: Does not work on the metal itself
methods_nb_nometal1: Cannot measure the metal itself (only contamination, films or rust on it)
methods_nb_dpS: Depth resolution is too coarse for the top few nm
methods_nb_layer: Deeper levels are measured by removing layers by electropolishing (destructive)
methods_why_only: Measures only certain elements, not the ones selected
methods_nb_only: Measures only certain elements (check that yours are among them)
methods_nb_coarse: The gauge volume is millimeter-sized, so changes within a shallow layer are averaged
home_feat_prep_desc: Sectioning, polishing and etching for {n} materials, and causes of common failures
about_prep: Look up how to prepare specimens for microstructural examination — carbon and stainless steels, cast iron, Al, Cu, Ti, solders, coatings, cemented carbides, ceramics and more — with grinding and polishing steps and etchants. Pick a defect (scratches, edge rounding, relief, stains, over-etching…) and your material to get likely causes and fixes in order; the selection can be shared as a URL. Hazards and precautions are given for each etchant.
prep_noscript: “Find the cause of a failure” needs JavaScript. All causes and fixes are listed for each defect in the failure table below.
prep_find_h: Find the cause of a failure
prep_pick: Choose the defect you see. If you also choose a material, causes are reordered for that material.
prep_count_m: {n} likely causes for {m}, most likely first
prep_up: Ranked higher because the material is:
prep_try: Find causes of failures for this material
prep_def_lead: Identify the defect from its appearance and check the causes in order of frequency. Material-specific tips also appear in each material's procedure.
prep_mat_lead: Steps are typical values for automatic machines from the sources; adjust while checking that each step has removed the previous scratches. Grit numbers are US (ANSI/CAMI) with European P grades in parentheses (conversion table under Grinding in the general sequence).
prep_not_h: Solutions not given on this page
prep_not_lead: The following are especially hazardous, so neither compositions nor procedures are given. They are used only where dedicated equipment, written procedures and training are in place.
prep_et_lead: Compositions are given in mL (volume) and g (mass); acids are concentrated reagent grade unless stated otherwise. Read the safety notes before using any etchant:
home_feat_measure_desc: Count grain size and phase fraction on your own micrograph, with uncertainty
about_measure: Open your own micrograph in the browser, set the scale, and count the grain size number G, mean intercept length and grains per unit area with the intercept and planimetric methods, or phase fractions with a point count. Field-to-field scatter, 95 % confidence interval and relative accuracy are given, and results can be saved as CSV and as a PNG with the marks. Practice on synthetic structures with known answers. Images are never sent anywhere.
measure_noscript: Measuring needs JavaScript. The counting rules, equations, grain size table, notes and FAQ below can be read without it.
measure_rules_lead: The mark types in the measuring tool follow these rules, checked against public material on ASTM E112 (grain size) and E562 (point count).
measure_fig_cap: How the test line (blue) meets grain boundaries and how each case scores: a crossing 1, a triple point 1.5, a tangent 1, a line end exactly on a boundary ½. For this line P = 1 + 1.5 + 1 + 1 + ½ = 5.
measure_fml_lead: Grain size numbers are calculated with the ASTM E112 equations. The formula collection has the same conversion:
measure_gtab_h: Grain size number, ℓ̄ and N_A
measure_gtab_lead: Values calculated with the ASTM E112 equations (checked at build time against Table 4 of E112). d̄ = 1/√N_A assumes square grains and is not the same as the mean intercept length ℓ̄.
measure_rel_lead: How to prepare the specimen, how to recognize the structure, and the equations explained.
measure_open_fmt: JPEG, PNG, WebP, BMP or GIF. Browsers often cannot read TIFF; export it as PNG first.
measure_open_bad: Could not read “{name}” as an image. Export it as PNG or JPEG and open it again.
measure_restore: Your previous measurement is still here (image “{name}”, {n} fields). The image itself is not stored; open the same image to continue.
measure_new_specimen: Switched to a different specimen (synthetic structure); the earlier fields were cleared.
measure_syn_h: Make a synthetic practice structure (known answer)
measure_syn_lead: After counting, check your result against the true value and against an ideal count. The settings and the random seed go into the URL, so the same image can be shared.
measure_syn_f: Area fraction of the dark phase
measure_syn_share: Copy the URL of this image
measure_view_empty: The image appears here once opened.
measure_cv_label: Image to measure. Arrow keys move, + and − zoom, 0 fits the whole image
measure_h_noimg: Open an image or make a synthetic practice structure.
measure_h_move: Drag to pan, pinch with two fingers to zoom (wheel with a mouse). Switch back to “Count” to count.
measure_h_icpt: Tap (click) where the lines meet grain boundaries. Choose the kind just below the image.
measure_h_plan: Tap the grains inside the figure and those cut by its outline. Choose the kind just below the image.
measure_h_pt: Tap grid points to assign each one to a phase.
measure_h_scroll: In “Count” mode, a vertical swipe scrolls the page.
measure_h_far: Too far from the lines. Tap on a line (zooming in helps).
measure_h_far_end: Tap near an end of a straight line.
measure_h_far_del: Tap near the mark to remove.
measure_h_scale_a: Tap one end of the scale bar.
measure_h_next: Next field: the pattern has moved to another place on the same image. To count on another photo, open that image.
measure_scale_noimg: Open an image to set its scale.
measure_scale_pick: Tap both ends of the scale bar
measure_scale_pick_lead: Tap both ends of the bar, then enter its length. Zoom in for precision.
measure_scale_mag_note: The width of the printed photo, or of the photo displayed at that magnification. The size on your screen after zooming cannot be used.
measure_scale_fovum: Specimen length covered by the photo width (µm)
measure_scale_none: No scale yet (intercept and planimetric values need it; the point count does not).
measure_scale_syn: The scale of the synthetic structure was set automatically. You can also practice calibrating with the scale bar in the strip below it.
measure_scale_syn_bar: Use the ends of the strip’s scale bar
measure_scale_carried: The scale of the previous image “{name}” was carried over. Set it again if the magnification differs.
measure_meth_noimg: Open an image to show the counting pattern.
measure_size_icpt: {p} % of the short side (total line length {L})
measure_locked: This field has marks, so the pattern is fixed (clear the marks, or change it in the next field).
measure_k_e: Line end on a boundary ½
measure_tally_icpt: This field: P = {p} (crossings {x}, triple points {j}, tangents {t}, ends {e}), line length {L}
measure_tally_plan: This field: inside {i}, cut {c}{k} → {n} grains, area {A}
measure_next: Finish this field and go to the next
measure_next_empty: This field has no marks yet. Count it before moving on (fields without marks are not used in the results).
measure_next_empty_pt: No point in this field has been assigned yet. If no point really falls on the phases you count, press again to record it as a field with zero hits.
measure_close: There is already a mark close by. Check that you have not counted the same place twice (use “Remove a mark” to delete it).
measure_qbar: Marks and count for this field
measure_ph_h: Phase names (choose the phase to assign just below the image)
measure_pt_fill: Assign all remaining points to this phase
measure_res_none: Results appear here once you count.
measure_r_lbar: Mean lineal intercept ℓ̄ (mean of field ℓ)
measure_r_grange: G (from the ends of the interval)
measure_r_sumn: Total grains (with ½ and corner terms)
measure_w_noscale: Some images have no scale; their fields give no value.
measure_w_one: With one field there is no scatter or confidence interval. Count more fields.
measure_w_zero: Fields with no intersections give no ℓ and were left out.
measure_w_low_icpt: Fields {list} have few intersections (E112 suggests 40–100 per placement, at least 50 with straight lines).
measure_w_few_icpt: E112 recommends three to five or more fields (five or more for the statistics).
measure_w_total_icpt: Total intersections: {n}. By the E112 guidance about 400 give 10 %RA.
measure_w_low_plan: Fields {list} have fewer than 50 grains in the figure (E112 suggests at least 50).
measure_w_high_plan: Some fields have more than 100 grains; counting errors grow, so use a smaller figure or a higher magnification.
measure_w_few_plan: E112 recommends at least three fields for the planimetric method.
measure_w_total_plan: Total grains: {n}. By the E112 guidance about 700 give 10 %RA.
measure_w_ra: Relative accuracy {ra} % exceeds 10 %. At the present scatter about {n} fields are needed for 10 %RA.
measure_w_ra_pt: {name}: relative accuracy {ra} % exceeds 10 %. At the present scatter about {n} fields are needed for 10 %RA.
measure_w_grid: {name}: for a fraction of {p} %, the E562 table suggests a {n}-point grid.
measure_w_pt_need: {name}: assuming independent points, about {n} fields are needed for 10 %RA.
measure_w_pt_30: E562 says at least 30 fields must be measured to calculate the 95 % confidence interval (now {n}). Until then, read the interval as a rough guide.
measure_est: This is an estimate. For formal assessment, follow the text of the standard and your organization’s procedures.
measure_save_png: Save the marked image as PNG
measure_copy_manual: Could not copy automatically; select the text below and copy it.
measure_rep_src: Equations: from public material on ASTM E112 (grain size) and ASTM E562 (point count).
measure_ans_lead: When you have finished counting, compare with the true values.
measure_ans_how: True values come from the geometry of the polygons and discs; “counted ideally” is a machine count on exactly your lines, figures and grids.
measure_ans_field_plan: field {i}: you inside {ui}, cut {uc}; ideal inside {vi}, cut {vc}
measure_ans_gnote: The true G of this structure is {gl} by the intercept method and {ga} by the planimetric method (planar polygons make the two differ; see “The synthetic practice structures”).
measure_ans_nodark: The “Dark phase” was deleted, so the point count cannot be checked. Make the synthetic structure again (press “Make”) to bring the dark phase back.
measure_ans_none: No fields have been counted on this synthetic structure yet.
measure_calc_h: Calculate the grain size number from counts (no image)
measure_calc_lead: Enter counts you have already made at the microscope or on a print, and the page gives the result with the same formulas and statistics as the image measurement. The intercept method takes the number of intersections, the test line length and the magnification; the planimetric method the grains inside and intercepted by the test figure, its area and the magnification; the point count the number of grid points and the points on the phase. As you add fields, the mean, standard deviation, 95 % confidence interval and relative accuracy appear.
measure_calc_eq_h: Formulas (lengths and areas on the image are converted to true size with the magnification)
measure_calc_eq_lead: L′ and A′ are the test line length and the test figure area measured on the image (a print or an image shown at a known magnification), and M is the magnification. P is the number of intersections (a triple point counts 1.5, a line end exactly touching a boundary ½); N_in is the number of grains inside the test figure and N_cut the number intercepted by it. With a rectangular figure the corner grains are not counted and 1 is added. Average the per-field ℓ, N_A or P_P, then convert the mean to a number.
measure_calc_noscript: The calculator needs JavaScript. The formulas are shown below, and the conversion between the grain size number, ℓ̄ and N_A can be read in the “Grain size number, ℓ̄ and N_A” table below.
measure_calc_u_mm: Length on the image (mm) and magnification
measure_calc_rect_note: With a rectangular figure, the grains at the four corners are not counted as intercepted grains; 1 is added per field instead (on average each corner grain lies ¼ inside). Nothing is added for a circle.
measure_calc_how_icpt: For each field, enter the number of intersections P (the total including triple points at 1.5 and line ends at ½) and the total test line length. For three concentric circles it is the sum of the three circumferences.
measure_calc_how_plan: For each field, enter the grains completely inside the test figure, the grains intercepted by its outline, the figure area on the image (mm²) and the magnification. A 5000 mm² circle at 100× is 0.5 mm² on the specimen.
measure_calc_how_pt: For each field, enter the number of grid points P_T and the number of points on the phase (a point on a boundary counts 0.5).
measure_calc_e_neg: enter a number of 0 or more
measure_calc_e_over: cannot exceed the number of grid points
measure_calc_e_bad: cannot be read as a number (use digits and a decimal point only)
measure_calc_none: Enter the counts of a field to see the result and the worked formulas here.
measure_calc_copy_link: Copy a link to these inputs
measure_calc_rep_title: Grain size number from counts — result (estimate)
measure_conv_h: Grain size conversion (G, ℓ̄, N_A, mean grain area)
measure_conv_lead: Enter any one of the grain size number G, the mean lineal intercept ℓ̄, the grains per mm² N_A, the grains per square inch at 100×, the mean grain area Ā or d̄ = √Ā, and the others are calculated with the ASTM E112 formulas.
measure_conv_eq_note: ℓ̄ in mm, N_A in mm⁻², Ā in µm² (10⁶ / N_A). n is the number of grains per square inch at 100× (0.064516 mm² on the specimen), which E112 defines as 2^(G−1). The ℓ̄–N_A relation assumes uniform equiaxed grains, as in E112 table 4, so the intercept and planimetric G of the same structure can differ slightly.
measure_conv_noscript: The converter needs JavaScript. Values for G = 0 to 10 are in the “Grain size number, ℓ̄ and N_A” table below.
measure_conv_hint: Type in any one box; the other boxes and the table below show the converted values.
measure_conv_in_dbar: d̄ = √Ā (µm, “average diameter” of the E112 table)
measure_conv_gjis: JIS G 0551 / ISO 643 number (area definition m = 8 × 2^G)
measure_conv_gjis_no: not given from ℓ̄ (the JIS intercept formula has not been checked)
measure_conv_diam: “Average grain size” has several definitions. Here d̄ is √Ā from the E112 table (assuming square grains) and the equivalent circle diameter is √(4Ā/π); both differ from the mean lineal intercept ℓ̄ (see “Mean grain diameter and the grain size number: points to watch”). For the same N_A, the JIS / ISO number is log₂(8/7.75) = 0.046 smaller than the ASTM number.
measure_conv_w_range: G = {g} is outside the range of the E112 tables (00 to 14). The conversion simply extends the formulas and is not a grain size number in the standard.
measure_gtab_more: n and Ā are also checked against E112 table 4.
